title: The Coffee Cup
dek: Four women murdered over a decade, investigated by agencies that never compared notes. A wrongly accused man died before he was cleared. The case finally broke on a discarded coffee cup, still flecked with cheese cracker crumbs.
cardBlurb: A decade of unsolved murders, split across jurisdictions that never connected the dots — until cold-case DNA work and a stolen coffee cup trace it all back to one man.
source: Timeline built from a Forensic Files episode summary and transcript describing the 1984–1986 Wichita Falls-area murders of Terry Sims, Toni Gibbs, Ellen Blau, and Tina Kimbrew, the wrongful prosecution of Danny Laughlin, and the 1990s cold-case investigation and DNA/fingerprint evidence that identified Faryion Wardrip, including his confession to a previously unknown fifth murder, Debra Taylor. Exact months for several 1980s and 1990s events are approximate, drawn from the episode's own account rather than court records.

wardrip.name: Faryion Wardrip
wardrip.role: Confessed serial killer, caught via DNA from a discarded coffee cup

laughlin.name: Danny Laughlin
laughlin.role: Wrongly tried for Toni Gibbs' murder; mistrial, then dismissed

gibbs.name: Toni Gibbs
gibbs.role: 23-year-old nurse, abducted after a night shift

taylor.name: Debra Taylor
taylor.role: Wife and mother, killed after meeting Wardrip at a bar

events.title: Terry Sims is murdered in her own home
events.summary: 21-year-old nurse Terry Sims answered a knock at her door; the man forced his way in. She fought back hard enough to leave a bloody fingerprint on her own shoe before she was sexually assaulted and stabbed to death.
events.detail: A semen sample was preserved from the scene for future DNA testing — technology that didn't yet exist in a form that could identify her killer, but that investigators had the foresight to save anyway.

quote.text: She is fighting so hard, so ferociously for her life, that he cuts a cord and ties her hands behind her back.

events.title: Toni Gibbs disappears after her night shift
events.summary: 23-year-old nurse Toni Gibbs vanished after working the night shift at Wichita General Hospital. Her car was found abandoned nearby, with no fingerprints or obvious clues inside.
events.detail: Four weeks later, her body was found in a field off US Route 281. An old bus 100 feet away held blood matching Toni — it appeared she'd been stabbed inside it, then crawled out into the field looking for help.

events.title: Danny Laughlin becomes a suspect
events.summary: 24-year-old Danny Laughlin, a local male stripper who'd met Toni weeks earlier, was seen riding a motorcycle near where her body was found. He failed a polygraph and made comments suggesting he knew details about the murder.
events.detail: Investigators also learned Laughlin had mentioned knowing where the field was located — circumstantial details that, combined, made him the prime suspect despite the lack of hard forensic evidence.

events.title: DNA testing comes back inconclusive
events.summary: Semen collected during Toni Gibbs' autopsy was compared to Laughlin's DNA. The results were inconclusive — neither clearing him nor confirming a match.
events.detail: Despite the lack of forensic confirmation, prosecutors charged Laughlin with the murder anyway, built largely on the circumstantial details investigators already had.

events.title: A deadlocked jury, then dismissal
events.summary: With no forensic evidence tying Laughlin to the crime, the case went to trial on circumstantial evidence alone. After two days of deliberation, the jury deadlocked — only one of twelve jurors believed he was guilty — and a mistrial was declared.
events.detail: Prosecutors chose not to retry the case. Laughlin walked away formally unconvicted, but with the accusation still hanging over him.

events.title: Ellen Blau is abducted and strangled
events.summary: 21-year-old Ellen Blau was walking to her car after a midnight shift when a man forced her into it and made her drive to a deserted field, where she was strangled.
events.detail: The killer drove her car back into town and abandoned it. Ellen's body wasn't found for days, and by then was too decomposed to confirm whether she'd been sexually assaulted — she could only be identified through dental records.

events.date: 16 months after Laughlin's case was dismissed
events.title: Tina Kimbrew is found dead in her apartment
events.summary: 21-year-old waitress Tina Kimbrew was found suffocated on her sofa — fibers from a pillow were found in her lungs. Neighbors reported seeing a tall, dark-haired man in a baseball cap leaving her apartment hours before.
events.detail: Danny Laughlin didn't match the witness description and wasn't considered a suspect in this case — this murder would turn out to belong to someone else entirely.

events.title: A man 400 miles away calls with a confession
events.summary: Faryion Wardrip, in Galveston, called police claiming to have information about Tina Kimbrew's murder. He'd known her from a bar where she worked, and where he says she'd supported him through a drug problem.
events.detail: Wardrip admitted to killing her, saying she reminded him of his ex-wife, who had recently ended their marriage. Police believe he confessed because he knew he'd been seen leaving her apartment.

quote.text: When the rage and all the violence was occurring, I saw her eyes. I saw her face. And I screamed how much I hated her.

events.title: A guilty plea, and 35 years
events.summary: Faryion Wardrip pleaded guilty to Tina Kimbrew's murder and was sentenced to 35 years in prison. At the time, no one connected him to the other unsolved Wichita Falls murders.
events.detail: In prison, Wardrip got his GED and said he found religion, later describing it as the point he decided to "come out better" than he went in.

events.title: Paroled, over the victim's family's objections
events.summary: Despite a decade of effort by Tina Kimbrew's father to keep him behind bars, Wardrip was released on parole after serving just 11 of his 35-year sentence. He moved to Olney, Texas, remarried, and became a respected member of his church community.
events.detail: Neighbors described him as trustworthy and upstanding — a reputation that existed entirely unaware of what investigators were about to uncover.

quote.text: The victims had no rights. I hate you every day for it.

events.title: A DA reopens the cold cases
events.summary: District Attorney Barry Macha asked investigator John Little to take a fresh look at the still-unsolved murders of Terry Sims, Toni Gibbs, and Ellen Blau. On a hunch, Macha had the lab compare the semen DNA from the Gibbs and Sims scenes.
events.detail: They matched — proving a single perpetrator was behind both murders. No one had made that connection before, because the cases had been investigated by three separate agencies that rarely communicated.

quote.text: We received word that they were, in fact, the semen from the same perpetrator. So we knew then that we had a serial murderer.

events.title: The old case files point to one name
events.summary: Reviewing the files, John Little found that Wardrip had once admitted, almost in passing, to knowing Ellen Blau — a lead that was never followed up. He also found that Blau's best friend lived near both Wardrip and the street where Terry Sims was killed.
events.detail: Little also discovered Wardrip had worked as a janitor at the same hospital as Toni Gibbs, and lived near where her car was abandoned — a web of coincidences that, once laid out together, pointed unmistakably in one direction.

quote.text: I mean, when I saw that in the file... it really snapped together for me at that point.

events.title: A stakeout for a coffee cup
events.summary: Little staked out the factory where Wardrip now worked, hoping to legally collect a discarded item carrying his DNA. He watched Wardrip finish a coffee break, then saw him throw the cup in a trash barrel.
events.detail: Among several discarded cups, Little identified the right one by the coffee left inside and cheese cracker crumbs on the rim — he'd watched Wardrip eating the same crackers minutes earlier.

quote.text: There was still some coffee in the bottom of his cup, and it had cheese cracker crumbs on the drinking rim... I said, this has got to be the cup.

events.title: An exact match, one in the world's population
events.summary: Lab analyst Judy Floyd extracted DNA from skin cells on the cup and matched it exactly to the semen profiles from both the Sims and Gibbs crime scenes. A rare DQ alpha marker made the match statistically close to unique.
events.detail: The combination of genetic markers in Wardrip's profile was so uncommon it would be expected to occur only once in the entire world's population — about as close to certainty as DNA evidence gets.

quote.text: I could see that his profile was an exact match to the profiles from the crime scenes.

events.title: A bloody fingerprint, finally matched
events.summary: The Austin crime lab compared the bloody fingerprint recovered from Terry Sims' shoe years earlier to Wardrip's prints. It was a match — positioned so low on the finger, near the palm, that it had been easy to miss in routine fingerprinting.
events.detail: Investigators believe the print was left when Wardrip pulled the shoes from Sims' feet with blood still on his hands.

events.title: Arrested, confronted, and a confession to a fifth murder
events.summary: Confronted with the DNA and fingerprint evidence, Wardrip confessed. Then, unprompted, he told investigators about a murder they didn't even know about: Debra Taylor, a wife and mother he'd met in a Fort Worth bar about two months after killing Toni Gibbs.
events.detail: Wardrip said Taylor's husband had briefly left the bar before them; when Taylor refused his advances in the parking lot, he killed her and dumped her body at a construction site. Her husband, Ken, had been informally suspected for 14 years and never charged — his life upended by suspicion for a murder he didn't commit.

quote.text: But John, there's one more. I believe that her name was Debra Taylor.

events.title: Danny Laughlin is cleared — too late
events.summary: The same DNA evidence that convicted Wardrip also formally exonerated Danny Laughlin, the man wrongly tried for Toni Gibbs' murder more than a decade earlier.
events.detail: Laughlin never learned he'd been cleared — he had died in a car accident three years before the exoneration came through.

events.title: Guilty plea, death sentence, nearly 15 years later
events.summary: Faryion Wardrip pleaded guilty to the murders and was sentenced to death by lethal injection, almost fifteen years after he killed Terry Sims.
events.detail: He later said he never believed he'd gotten away with it — he knew he'd left evidence behind, and was puzzled that his name, which had surfaced in the files as early as 1986, wasn't connected sooner.

quote.text: I really was a serial killer. Mistakes were made. But the one that was not made was to quit or to give up.
